methodological_rigor.justification: Two-center retrospective matched cohort with sequential matching by age and diagnosis year (+/- 2 years) comparing 57 pSMM to 57 dnMM patients. Strengths: pre-specified primary endpoints (end-organ damage, PFS), clear IMWG and SLiM-CRAB criteria, reverse censoring for follow-up, differences reported as similar when adjusted for year of diagnosis, age, gender, ISS, and R-ISS. Weaknesses: small sample, retrospective single-region design, only two matching variables leaving substantial confounding risk (particularly lead-time and length-time bias, which the authors acknowledge), and no formal propensity score analysis. Statistical methods (Chi-square/Fisher, Mann-Whitney, Kaplan-Meier, log-rank) are appropriate for the descriptive comparisons, though multivariate Cox details are not fully reported and effect estimates for survival lack HRs with CIs.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Matched retrospective cohort classifies as Oxford LoE 4 (low-quality cohort). Clinical relevance is high for practicing hematologists because the question (does SMM surveillance reduce end-organ damage and improve survival?) is directly actionable. Findings (44% vs 72% irreversible complications; 3-year OS 92% vs 76%) inform current surveillance practices and contextualize the AQUILA trial results for early daratumumab intervention in high-risk SMM. Findings may influence surveillance intensification recommendations.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE-applicable observational cohort reporting is mostly present: eligibility criteria, IMWG reference definitions, outcome definitions (PFS, OS from active MM diagnosis), and statistical methods are clear. Limitations section is transparent about sample size, retrospective design, and potential confounders. Missing elements include formal participant flow diagram, details on handling of missing data, explicit HR with CI for multivariate adjustments, and a data availability statement. Institutional clinical data likely cannot be shared.

novelty_literature.justification: Prior studies (Goyal 2019 Mayo, Go 2015 SEER-Medicare) have reported OS advantages for precursor-detected MM vs dnMM, and the authors cite these. The novel contribution is the focus on end-organ damage as the primary outcome (rather than OS alone), detailed characterization of bone disease subtypes, and contextualization against the recent AQUILA trial findings (cited as [7] Dimopoulos 2025). Meaningful but not first-in-class; extends prior OS-focused comparisons to include irreversible complications.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-written manuscript with logical structure, clear tables and figures references, and a thoughtful discussion that situates findings within the current therapeutic landscape (AQUILA trial). Limitations are candidly addressed. Some minor redundancy and a few grammatical issues, but overall communication is strong.

key_strengths: Clinically relevant question addressing whether SMM surveillance prevents irreversible end-organ damage, extending prior OS-focused comparisons
Matched cohort design (age, diagnosis year) with adjustment for ISS/R-ISS, reducing some confounding
Pre-specified composite end-organ damage endpoint (44% vs 72%, p=0.002) with biologically coherent bone involvement breakdowns
Thoughtful discussion integrating findings with the recent AQUILA trial context for high-risk SMM treatment
Transparent acknowledgment of lead-time/length-time bias and retrospective design limitations
key_concerns: Small sample (n=57 per arm) limits precision, particularly for survival and multivariate analyses
Lead-time and length-time bias may substantially inflate PFS and OS differences; the authors note but do not quantitatively adjust for these biases
Matching only on age and diagnosis year; no formal propensity score analysis
Multivariate Cox details (HRs with CIs) not fully reported for adjusted survival analyses
Single geographic region (two centers in Israel) limits generalizability
No data availability statement or code sharing
chief_reviewer.rationale: Clinically meaningful matched cohort study with appropriate statistical framing and strong relevance to current SMM management debates; moderate confounding risk and small sample size place it at Tier 3 with minor revisions to expand bias discussion and report multivariate estimates.
